english: moreover; on top of that; what's more
usage: And on top of that, it even rained
Adds a second, often worse, point onto what was just said
Frequently pairs with -은/는데 to stack reasons
especially at a time like now
Can stress that the added fact makes things harder
Leans toward piling on bad news; for neutral addition use 게다가/더욱이
examples: 일이 많은데 더구나 사람까지 부족해서 야근이 잦아요.
There's a lot of work, and on top of that we're short-staffed, so we often work late.
Stacks a second burden onto the first
그 식당은 비싸요. 더구나 맛도 별로였어요.
That restaurant is expensive. What's more, the food wasn't even good.
Adds a second complaint
초보자에게는 어려운 책이에요. 더구나 분량도 많고요.
It's a hard book for beginners. Moreover, it's quite long too.
Written-leaning addition with -고요 softening
nuance: 더구나 stacks an additional fact onto the previous statement, usually intensifying a negative situation ('and to make matters worse'). It is close to 게다가 and 더욱이 but feels slightly more formal and more strongly tied to compounding difficulty. Use it when the second point makes the overall picture more extreme, not for simply listing neutral items.
mistakes: Using 더구나 to add a positive, neutral item (e.g. a plain shopping list) where 그리고/게다가 fits better.
Treating it as a sentence object; it is an adverb that opens or links a clause, not a noun.

usage: Singles out one item from a larger set
Boosts a quality: 특히 중요해요 (especially important)
Common collocation to narrow down further
특히나 is a slightly stronger, more colloquial variant
examples: 저는 과일을 좋아하는데, 특히 딸기를 제일 좋아해요.
I like fruit, and I especially like strawberries the most.
Picks out one favorite from a category
이번 시험은 특히 듣기 부분이 어려웠어요.
This time the exam was especially hard in the listening section.
Highlights one part as standing out
주말에는, 특히 일요일에는 사람이 정말 많아요.
On weekends, especially on Sundays, it's really crowded.
Narrows a general statement to a specific case
nuance: 특히 points to one member of a group as standing out from the rest, equivalent to 'especially' or 'in particular.' Unlike 특별히, which emphasizes that something is done in a special or deliberate way, 특히 simply selects the most notable item from a set. It naturally follows a general statement and then zooms in on the exception.
mistakes: Confusing 특히 (singling out from a group) with 특별히 (doing something specially/on purpose).
Placing it so far from the highlighted item that it's unclear what is being singled out.

usage: States one's usual or dominant habit
Marks the typical place something happens
Identifies the chief object or target
Blends 'most of the time' and 'for the most part'
examples: 저는 주말에 주로 집에서 쉬어요.
On weekends I mostly rest at home.
Describes a typical pattern of behavior
이 카페에는 주로 학생들이 와요.
Mostly students come to this cafe.
States the dominant type of customer
점심은 주로 회사 근처에서 간단히 먹어요.
I usually eat lunch simply near the office.
Marks a habitual choice without claiming 'always'
nuance: 주로 means 'mainly/mostly' and describes what is typical or dominant, leaving room for exceptions. It overlaps with 보통 (usually) and 대부분 (for the most part), but 주로 emphasizes the principal case among options rather than pure frequency. Use it to describe habits, typical locations, or the main kind of thing involved.
mistakes: Using 주로 to mean 'absolutely always'; it implies a tendency, not 100%.
Swapping it with 주로/주류 (mainstream) as a noun; here it is strictly an adverb.

usage: Softens an adjective: 비교적 쉬워요 (relatively easy)
Hedges a claim about size or extent
비교적 stays adverbial; do not conjugate it
examples: 이 동네는 비교적 조용한 편이에요.
This neighborhood is relatively quiet.
Hedges the claim against other areas
오늘은 비교적 일이 적어서 일찍 퇴근했어요.
Today there was comparatively little work, so I left early.
Implies 'less than usual'
한국어 발음은 비교적 규칙적이라서 배우기 쉬워요.
Korean pronunciation is relatively regular, so it's easy to learn.
Softens a generalization for learners
nuance: 비교적 means 'relatively/comparatively' and hedges an adjective or quantity against an implied standard. It tells the listener that the quality holds only in comparison, not absolutely, which makes statements sound more careful and intermediate. It is more formal and measured than 꽤 or 좀, and unlike 별로 it carries no negative bias.
mistakes: Conjugating it as 비교적이에요; 비교적 is an adverb and should modify, e.g., 비교적 쉬워요.
Using it where there is truly no point of comparison; a baseline (even implicit) should exist.

english: on the whole; generally; for the most part
usage: Gives an overall impression with minor exceptions
대체로 stresses the general trend, not a count
examples: 설문 결과를 보면 사람들은 대체로 새 정책에 찬성해요.
Looking at the survey, people generally support the new policy.
Summarizes a broad trend
호텔은 대체로 깨끗했지만 와이파이가 좀 느렸어요.
The hotel was on the whole clean, though the Wi-Fi was a bit slow.
Gives an overall verdict with one exception
그 강의는 대체로 이해하기 쉬운 편이었어요.
That lecture was, for the most part, fairly easy to follow.
Hedges an evaluation
nuance: 대체로 gives an overall, big-picture judgment ('on the whole'), acknowledging that small exceptions may exist. It pairs naturally with evaluations and summaries and is more analytical than 보통. Compared with 주로 (which picks the dominant case), 대체로 averages over the whole situation to state a general tendency.
mistakes: Using 대체로 for a single concrete instance; it describes overall tendencies, not one event.
Confusing it with 대체 (= 도대체, 'on earth') used in questions; the meanings are unrelated.

usage: States what is usually true as a rule
examples: 일반적으로 한국에서는 식사 중에 어른이 먼저 수저를 들어요.
Generally in Korea, elders pick up their spoon first during a meal.
States a cultural norm as a rule
일반적으로 이런 증상은 며칠이면 좋아져요.
Generally, symptoms like these get better within a few days.
Gives a typical expectation
일반적으로 말하면, 경험이 많을수록 일이 수월해져요.
Generally speaking, the more experience you have, the easier the work becomes.
Frames a broad generalization
nuance: 일반적으로 introduces a general rule or what is typically the case, much like 'in general' or 'typically.' It is more formal and explanatory than 보통 and is common in writing, explanations, and academic-leaning speech. It often sets up a norm that can later be contrasted with exceptions (예외적으로).
mistakes: Dropping the -으로 and saying 일반적 alone as an adverb; the adverbial form needs -으로.
Using it for personal habits ('I generally…'); for that, 주로/보통 sound more natural.

usage: 특별히 = in a special way; 특히 = among others
examples: 오늘은 손님이 오셔서 특별히 음식을 많이 준비했어요.
We have guests today, so I specially prepared a lot of food.
Emphasizes deliberate, out-of-the-ordinary effort
특별히 가고 싶은 곳은 없어요. 아무 데나 괜찮아요.
There's no place I particularly want to go. Anywhere is fine.
Common in negative sentences
선생님이 저를 특별히 챙겨 주셔서 감사했어요.
The teacher looked after me especially well, so I was grateful.
Marks special, individualized treatment
nuance: 특별히 means doing or feeling something in a special, deliberate, or out-of-the-ordinary way, and in negative sentences it softens to 'not particularly.' This contrasts with 특히, which simply singles out one item from a group. Choose 특별히 when the emphasis is on the special manner or intent, and especially favor it in '없어요/않아요' patterns.
mistakes: Using 특별히 where you mean 'among these, especially X'; that calls for 특히.
Forgetting that 특별히 + negative is the idiomatic way to say 'not really / nothing in particular.'

usage: Flags the single most important point
Common lead-in to a key point
Stresses priority in order and importance
examples: 건강이 무엇보다 중요하다고 생각해요.
I think health is more important than anything.
Ranks one thing above all others
여러 이유가 있지만, 무엇보다 가족과 가까워서 이 동네를 골랐어요.
There are several reasons, but above all I chose this neighborhood to be near family.
Highlights the decisive reason
새 직장은 무엇보다 분위기가 좋아서 마음에 들어요.
I like my new workplace above all because the atmosphere is good.
Points to the top factor in a judgment
nuance: 무엇보다 (often 무엇보다도) elevates one point above everything else, like 'above all' or 'more than anything.' It is a natural way to mark your top priority or the most decisive factor when several exist. Slightly emphatic and common in both speech and writing, it pairs especially well with 중요하다 and reasons for a choice.
mistakes: Treating 무엇보다 as a comparison of two concrete nouns; it ranks one point over all others, not just one rival.
Reading it literally as 'than what'; it functions as a fixed expression meaning 'above all.'

english: never; by no means (with a negative)
usage: never V; by no means V
Must be paired with a negative predicate
결코 쉽지 않아요 (by no means easy)
결코 cannot stand with a positive verb
결코 is more written/formal than 절대로
examples: 저는 그 약속을 결코 잊지 않을 거예요.
I will never forget that promise.
Strong, formal negation of a future action
이건 결코 쉬운 결정이 아니었어요.
This was by no means an easy decision.
Emphatically denies a quality
그분은 결코 그런 말을 할 사람이 아니에요.
He is by no means the kind of person who would say that.
Firmly rejects a possibility
nuance: 결코 is an emphatic negative adverb meaning 'never / by no means,' and it must co-occur with a negative ending such as -지 않다 or 아니다. It is more formal and emphatic than 절대로 and is common in writing, declarations, and firm statements. Because it inherently signals negation, sentences feel incomplete or wrong if the predicate is positive.
mistakes: Pairing 결코 with an affirmative predicate; it requires a negative (-지 않다/아니다/없다).
Using it casually in light conversation where 절대(로) or 전혀 would sound more natural.

english: finally; at last; in the end
usage: Caps a long process with its result
after a long N, at last
Often follows a phrase of long effort/waiting
마침내 is more literary; 드디어 more spoken
examples: 몇 년 동안 준비한 끝에 마침내 시험에 합격했어요.
After years of preparation, I finally passed the exam.
Marks the climactic result of long effort
오래 기다린 소식이 마침내 도착했어요.
The long-awaited news finally arrived.
Emphasizes the awaited outcome
여러 번 실패했지만 마침내 원하던 결과를 얻었어요.
I failed several times, but in the end I got the result I wanted.
Closes a struggle with success
nuance: 마침내 means 'finally/at last' and frames an outcome as the culmination of a long process, effort, or wait. It is more literary and emphatic than the everyday 드디어, and it strongly implies that the result was hard-won. Use it to give weight to a meaningful conclusion, often after phrases like '오랜 노력 끝에.'
mistakes: Using 마침내 for trivial 'and then finally' sequencing; it implies a significant, awaited result.
Confusing it with 마침 ('as it happens / just in time'), which has a different meaning.

english: on the contrary; conversely; the other way around
usage: 반대로 하다 = do it the other way around
Marks a contrast with a stated reference
examples: 형은 활발한데, 반대로 동생은 아주 조용해요.
The older brother is outgoing; conversely, the younger one is very quiet.
Contrasts two people directly
쉬울 거라고 생각했는데 반대로 정말 어려웠어요.
I thought it would be easy, but on the contrary it was really hard.
Reverses an expectation
설명서와 반대로 조립해서 다시 해야 했어요.
I assembled it the opposite way from the manual, so I had to redo it.
Means 'in the reverse manner'
nuance: 반대로 introduces an opposite case or a reversal, covering both 'on the contrary' (contrasting facts) and 'the other way around' (reversed manner/direction). It is more concrete than the abstract connector 반면(에), often pointing to a literal opposite action or a flipped expectation. Use it to flip a statement, contrast two parties, or describe doing something in reverse.
mistakes: Using 반대로 only as a pure clause-connector where 반면(에) fits; 반대로 leans toward a literal opposite.
Forgetting the marker in 'N과/와 반대로' when contrasting with a specific reference point.

usage: solely for the sake of N
examples: 그동안 오로지 가족만 생각하며 일해 왔어요.
All this time I've worked thinking only of my family.
Stresses single-minded focus
이 결과는 오로지 본인의 노력 덕분이에요.
This result is entirely thanks to your own effort.
Attributes a cause to one factor alone
그 선수는 오로지 우승만을 목표로 훈련했어요.
That athlete trained aiming solely at the championship.
Marks one exclusive goal
nuance: 오로지 means 'only/solely/entirely' and emphasizes single-minded exclusivity, often paired with -만 or -뿐. It is more emphatic and emotional than the plainer 오직, suggesting wholehearted devotion or a single cause. Use it to highlight that one purpose, person, or factor stands alone with nothing else involved.
mistakes: Treating 오로지 like the counting adverb 'only X items'; for quantities use 단지/겨우, not 오로지.
Dropping the supporting -만/-뿐 where the sentence needs it to complete the 'only' meaning.

english: in a word; in short; to put it simply
usage: Sums up with a single label
to put it in one word
Common fuller form before a summary
한마디로 is punchier and more spoken
examples: 그 영화는 한마디로 시간 낭비였어요.
That movie was, in a word, a waste of time.
Compresses a judgment into one phrase
한마디로 말하면, 준비가 부족했던 거예요.
To put it simply, we just weren't prepared enough.
Leads into a blunt summary
새 제도는 한마디로 누구에게나 공평해요.
The new system is, in short, fair to everyone.
Gives a one-line takeaway
nuance: 한마디로 means 'in a word / in short' and signals that you are about to condense everything into one blunt summary or label. It is conversational and often a bit emphatic or evaluative, used right before delivering your bottom line. Compared with the more neutral 요약하면, 한마디로 sounds punchier and more opinionated.
mistakes: Following 한마디로 with a long, multi-clause explanation; it promises a short, single takeaway.
Reading it literally as 'with one word said'; it works as a fixed discourse marker meaning 'in short.'
